## Web Development Company in Pune: Why Your New Website Is Not on Google, and How to Fix "Crawled – Currently Not Indexed"

Most new business websites that "do not show on Google" fall into one of four buckets: Google has not found the site yet, Google found it but has not fetched the pages, Google fetched the pages and decided not to keep them, or something on the site is telling Google to stay away. Each bucket has a different fix, and Google Search Console tells you which one you are in. If you are paying a web development company in Pune to build or maintain your site, learning to read that one report will save you weeks of guessing and a lot of awkward phone calls.

This guide is for owners of clinics, coaching classes, manufacturing units, shops, NGOs and service firms who launched a site and cannot find it by searching their own business name or their main service. We will walk through the Page indexing report, explain each status in plain language, show what is within your control and what is not, and give you a realistic checklist. We do not promise that any page will be indexed by a given date. Google decides that, and no agency can honestly guarantee it.

### First, confirm the problem is really indexing

Before you open any tool, check three simple things, because many "not on Google" complaints are something else.

**Search for your exact domain.** Type `site:yourdomain.com` into Google. This is a rough check, not an audit, but if it returns nothing at all for a site that has been live for weeks, indexing is a real concern. If it returns pages, the site is indexed and your issue is ranking, which is a different problem with a different fix.

**Search for your business name.** A brand-new site will often appear for its exact name before it appears for anything competitive. Appearing for your name but not for "dentist in Kothrud" is a ranking and relevance question, not an indexing one.

**Check you are not looking at a staging copy.** Agencies often build on a temporary address and then move the site. If the live site still carries a "discourage search engines" setting from the build period, Google is being asked not to index it. We cover that below.

### Set up Search Console before anything else

Google Search Console is free and is the only source that shows how Google itself sees your site. Add your site as a property and verify ownership. A domain property covers every version of your address (http, https, www and non-www) in one view, which avoids the common confusion of looking at the wrong version.

Make sure the person who owns the business, not only the developer, is an owner of the property. We have seen sites where the only verified user was a freelancer who has since moved on. Our guide to [website handover and ownership](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-handover-ownership-checklist-2026/) lists the accounts you should hold yourself.

Then open **Indexing → Pages**. This is the Page indexing report. Google documents it in its [Search Console Help pages](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7440203). It splits your known URLs into "Indexed" and "Not indexed" and lists a reason for each group of not-indexed pages. Those reasons are the map for the rest of this article.

### Reading the statuses in plain language

Google uses a handful of status labels. They sound alarming, and several are completely normal. Here is what each one generally means.

| Status | What it generally means | Is it a problem? |
|---|---|---|
| Discovered – currently not indexed | Google knows the URL exists but has not fetched it yet | Often temporary on a new site; persistent for weeks is worth investigating |
| Crawled – currently not indexed | Google fetched the page and chose not to add it to the index for now | Needs a look: usually about quality, duplication or value |
| Excluded by "noindex" tag | The page tells Google not to index it | Fine if intentional; a serious error if not |
| Blocked by robots.txt | Your robots.txt file stops Google fetching the page | Fine for admin areas; an error for real pages |
| Page with redirect | The URL redirects elsewhere | Normal; the target is what gets indexed |
| Duplicate, Google chose different canonical | Google considers another URL the main version | Check that its choice matches yours |
| Not found (404) | The URL does not exist | Normal for deleted pages; a problem if it is a page you want |

The two statuses that cause the most worry are the first two, so we will spend the most time on them.

### "Discovered – currently not indexed": patience, then plumbing

This status means Google has heard about the URL, usually from your sitemap or a link, but has not yet fetched it. In a public video, Google's Martin Splitt described the Discovered status as not necessarily an error that needs immediate attention. For a site that is a few days or a couple of weeks old, waiting is a legitimate first response.

If the status persists for weeks, look at three things.

**Server health.** If your hosting is slow or frequently unavailable, Google may fetch less often so it does not overload the server. Cheap shared hosting that times out under load is a genuine cause. Our guide to [server response time, CDN and caching](/blog/web-development-company-pune-server-response-ttfb-cdn-caching-2026/) explains how to check this, and our refreshed [hosting guide](/blog/best-web-hosting-india-2026/) explains what to ask a host.

**Internal links.** A page that no other page links to is easy for Google to deprioritise. Every page you want indexed should be reachable from your menu or from other relevant pages within a few clicks. A "Services" page that links to each service page is better than ten service pages that exist only in a sitemap.

**Site size and perceived value.** A brand-new domain with no external links is crawled cautiously. Earning a few genuine mentions, such as a Google Business Profile, a listing on a relevant association site or a local news mention, helps Google discover and trust the site. Do not buy links. Google's spam policies, published at [Google Search Central](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies), treat link schemes as a violation.

### "Crawled – currently not indexed": the harder one

This means Google fetched the page, read it, and decided not to add it to the index for now. It does not mean there is an error on the page. The Wix help centre makes the same point about its own sites, and it applies everywhere. It also does not mean the decision is permanent. Pages can move in and out of this status.

Because Google has chosen not to explain its decision page by page, you have to reason from the evidence. In our experience, the causes cluster into a few groups.

#### Thin or near-duplicate pages

Imagine a Pune service firm with a page for each locality: "Website design in Baner", "Website design in Aundh", "Website design in Wakad", each with the same three paragraphs and the locality name swapped. Google can recognise that these pages add little over each other. The fix is not to rewrite them with different synonyms. It is to ask whether each page has something genuinely different: different projects, different customer questions, different services, different contact details. If it does not, merge the pages into one strong page and redirect the others to it.

Google's guidance on helpful, people-first content, at [Google Search Central](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content), is the right test. Ask whether a visitor who lands on the page would feel they learned something they could not learn from the page next to it.

#### Pages with almost no content

A "Services" page that contains a heading and a button, or a product page with only a photo and a price, gives Google little to index. This is common on sites built from page-builder templates where the placeholder text was deleted and nothing replaced it. Add the content a buyer would want: what is included, who it is for, how long it takes, how to start, and the questions people ask before buying. Our article on [website content readiness](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-content-copy-photos-launch-delays-2026/) covers why content is usually what delays a launch.

#### Content that exists only after JavaScript runs

Some modern sites send the browser an almost empty page and build the content with JavaScript. Google can render JavaScript, but rendering is a second step that can be delayed, and any failure leaves Google with an empty page. If your site is built this way, check what Google sees using the URL Inspection tool in Search Console: inspect a URL, view the crawled page and look at the rendered HTML and screenshot. If key text or links are missing there, ask your developer to server-render or pre-render the page. We pre-render our own site's pages for exactly this reason.

#### Duplicate versions of the same page

If your page loads at several addresses, for example with and without a trailing slash, with tracking parameters or on both http and https, Google may pick one and drop the others. Check that every page declares a single canonical address and that the alternatives redirect to it. Our guide on [404 errors, redirects and broken links](/blog/web-development-company-pune-404-errors-redirects-broken-links-2026/) shows how to find these.

#### Low perceived value for the site as a whole

Sometimes the honest answer is that a page is one of many similar pages and Google does not see a reason to keep it. A blog with fifty short posts that repeat the same advice, or a catalogue of near-identical products, can see a large share of pages parked in this status while the strongest pages are indexed. Quality, not quantity, is the lever. Fewer, better pages usually perform better than many thin ones.

### The accidental blocks: noindex and robots.txt

Some indexing failures are self-inflicted and quick to fix. Check these early.

**The WordPress "Discourage search engines" setting.** In WordPress, under Settings → Reading, there is a checkbox that asks search engines not to index the site. Developers tick it during the build so unfinished work does not appear in Google. If nobody unticks it at launch, the site stays hidden. This is one of the most common launch mistakes and the easiest to fix. WordPress's own wording says it is up to search engines to honour the request, but Google does.

**A noindex tag left in the page.** A noindex directive can sit in the page's HTML or in the HTTP header. SEO plugins also let you set noindex per page. In Search Console, the "Excluded by noindex tag" status lists the affected URLs. If a page you want in Google is on that list, remove the tag and request indexing.

**A robots.txt that blocks too much.** The robots.txt file sits at the root of your domain. A single line such as `Disallow: /` blocks everything. Developers sometimes leave this on after staging. Open `yourdomain.com/robots.txt` and read it. If you see a blanket disallow on a live site, ask for it to be corrected. If you use a CDN or security service that manages robots.txt for you, check its settings as well. Our articles on [robots.txt and AI crawlers](/blog/web-development-company-pune-ai-crawlers-robots-txt-2026/) explain how to edit this file without blocking Google by accident.

**Password protection or login walls.** Pages behind a login cannot be indexed. If your whole site sits behind a maintenance-mode plugin, the plugin may send a status that tells Google to come back later or that the page does not exist. Check that maintenance mode is off.

### Sitemaps: useful, but not magic

A sitemap is a file listing the URLs you want Google to know about. Submit it in Search Console under Indexing → Sitemaps. Google explains the format and purpose in its [sitemap documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview).

Two points matter. First, a sitemap helps discovery but does not force indexing. Submitting a sitemap full of thin pages will not make them indexable. Second, keep the sitemap clean: include only pages you want indexed, with the correct address and no redirects, errors or noindex pages. A sitemap that lists broken or blocked URLs sends mixed signals and clutters the report. If your site was recently restructured, our guide to [website structure and sitemap planning](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-structure-sitemap-planning-2026/) shows how to decide which pages belong.

### Using the URL Inspection tool well

The URL Inspection tool is the closest thing to asking Google directly about a page. Paste a full address into the search bar at the top of Search Console. It tells you whether the page is indexed, when it was last crawled, which canonical Google chose, whether the page is mobile-friendly, and whether it is blocked.

You can then click "Request indexing". Use this sparingly. It adds the URL to a queue for crawling, but it does not guarantee indexing, and there are daily limits. It is sensible for a new key page, such as your homepage or a main service page, or after you have fixed a real problem. It is not a way to push hundreds of low-value pages. If a page is declined repeatedly, the cause is in the page or the site, and re-requesting will not change that.

The "Test live URL" option fetches the page now rather than showing the last crawl. Use it after a fix to confirm Google can now see what you expect.

### A realistic checklist, in order

Work through these in sequence. Stop when the problem is solved.

1. **Verify ownership in Search Console** with a domain property, and make sure the business owner holds an owner role.
2. **Confirm the site is not blocking itself.** Check the WordPress Reading setting, view the page source for a noindex tag, and read robots.txt.
3. **Submit a clean sitemap** listing only pages you want indexed.
4. **Inspect the homepage and one key service page** with the URL Inspection tool. Read what Google sees, including the rendered view.
5. **Check internal links.** Every important page should be linked from the menu, footer or a relevant page.
6. **Review content on any page in "Crawled – currently not indexed".** Ask whether it is thin, duplicated or empty. Improve, merge or remove.
7. **Check canonicals and redirects** so each page has one address.
8. **Check server health.** If the site is slow or often down, fix the hosting before anything else.
9. **Wait.** After real fixes, allow a few weeks and review the report again. Do not repeat requests daily.
10. **Earn genuine links and mentions** through a complete Google Business Profile, relevant directory listings and press or association mentions.

### What you cannot control

It is worth being honest about the limits. Google indexes a subset of what it crawls, and a new domain starts with little trust. There is no formula that guarantees a particular page will be indexed on a particular date. If an agency promises "guaranteed indexing in 24 hours", treat that as a warning sign, since indexing is Google's decision. What you can do is remove obstacles, give Google clear and useful pages, and make the site easy to crawl.

### Worked example: a coaching class site that was invisible

Consider a hypothetical coaching class in Pune that launched a site with eight pages. Four weeks later, only the homepage appeared in search, and only for the class name. The owner assumed the agency had done something wrong. We use this as an illustration of how the checklist works; it is not a real client.

In Search Console, the Page indexing report showed three pages as "Discovered – currently not indexed" and four as "Crawled – currently not indexed". That split matters. The three discovered pages had no links from the menu, because the theme's menu listed only the homepage and contact page. The four crawled pages were course pages with two short sentences each and a "Enquire now" button.

The fix was ordinary. The developer added the course pages to the main menu and linked each from a "Courses" overview. The owner wrote real content for each course: who it is for, the syllabus outline, batch timings, how admission works, and answers to the questions parents usually ask. The sitemap was resubmitted, and the two most important pages were inspected and requested. Nothing here is clever; it is making the pages worth indexing and easy to reach. Outcomes vary, and we cannot say when each page would appear.

### When to involve your developer, and what to ask

Some fixes are yours: writing content, improving pages, earning mentions. Others need a developer: server rendering, canonical tags, redirects, robots.txt and hosting. When you raise the issue, be specific. Instead of "Google is not showing my site", send this.

- A screenshot of the Page indexing report with the status and count.
- Two or three example URLs with the exact status.
- The result of URL Inspection for one of them, including whether the page is blocked and what canonical Google chose.
- A clear request: "Please confirm noindex, robots.txt and canonical settings for these pages, and tell me what the rendered HTML contains."

A competent developer can answer those questions within a day. If the answers are vague, that tells you something about the agency too. Our [guide to website maintenance plans](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-maintenance-plan-what-to-include-2026/) explains what ongoing monitoring should include so indexing issues are caught early rather than discovered months after launch.

### Monitoring after the fix

Indexing is not a one-time task. After the first round of fixes, check the Page indexing report every few weeks. Watch the trend, not individual pages. A rising count of indexed pages and a stable count of not-indexed pages with expected reasons is healthy. A sudden jump in "Not found (404)" or "Excluded by noindex" after a redesign or plugin update is a signal to investigate quickly.

Search Console's performance data is also limited in how far back it goes, so if you want a long-term record, export it regularly. Google's [Performance report help page](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/7576553) describes what the report includes and its time ranges.

For readers who also care about being seen in AI search features, our article on [Search Console and AI visibility](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-search-console-ai-visibility-2026/) covers how to read those reports without over-interpreting them.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why is my new website not showing on Google?

The usual reasons are that Google has not yet discovered or crawled the site, that it crawled the pages and chose not to index them, or that a setting such as noindex or robots.txt blocks them. Open Search Console's Page indexing report to see which applies. A very new domain can also simply need time.

### What does "Crawled – currently not indexed" mean?

It means Google fetched the page but has not added it to its index for now. It is not an error message. It often points to thin, duplicated or low-value content, or to a page that is hard to reach from the rest of the site. Improve or merge the page, then review the report after a few weeks.

### How long does Google take to index a new website?

There is no fixed time. It can be days for a simple site with clear links and a submitted sitemap, and longer for a new domain with little content. Be wary of anyone who guarantees a date, because indexing is Google's decision.

### Does submitting a sitemap guarantee indexing?

No. A sitemap helps Google discover your URLs but does not force it to index them. A clean sitemap that lists only valuable, working pages supports discovery. It cannot rescue pages that are thin, blocked or duplicated.

### Should I click "Request indexing" repeatedly?

No. Use it for key pages and after a genuine fix. Repeated requests do not change Google's assessment of a page, and there are daily limits. If a page keeps being declined, work on the page or the site rather than on the request.

## Where to Start

Open Search Console, read the Page indexing report, and sort your not-indexed pages by reason. Check the accidental blocks first because they are fast. Then look at the content of each page in "Crawled – currently not indexed" and decide whether to improve, merge or remove it.
